findings.root_cause:
src/cochem_pipeline/coding.py:204-218 (read_workspace) gets each entry's metadata from os.scandir's DirEntry.stat(follow_symlinks=False) at line 210. It then refuses any file whose st_nlink != 1 at line 217. On Windows, DirEntry.stat is built from FindFirstFile/FindNextFile directory data, and st_nlink, st_ino and st_dev are always 0 there. Python documents this under os.DirEntry.stat: "always set to zero. Call os.stat() to get these attributes." So every ordinary file fails the check with 'Worker created a non-regular or hard-linked file'.

read_workspace runs right after the native CLI returns successfully, for every native coding kind (coding.py:440-445). That includes CODE_PLAN, the first stage. So every coding workflow fails at its first native stage, after the inference has already been spent. It runs again after the controller applies a CODE_EDIT (coding.py:467).

The installed r4 package has the same code: lines 199-227 match byte for byte, with the defect at installed coding.py:210.

This is the only DirEntry.stat use anywhere in src/. Every other link-count, inode or device check goes through Path.stat/Path.lstat/os.fstat, which return real values on Windows.

The tests missed it for three reasons:
- The only test that touches read_workspace (pipeline_tests/test_coding_boundaries.py:129-137) checks only the refusal. On Windows it passes because everything is refused.
- No test calls read_workspace on an ordinary file on any platform.
- All CodingFixture-based coding tests skip on Windows unless the run is SYSTEM.

findings.root_cause:
CHAPTER_DRAFT acceptance asks the model to copy back data the controller already owns. JobStore._chapter (store.py:730-746) validates the model's wbs_tasks_defined and then requires every manifest-declared task to come back as a Python-equal dict: `accepted = {task['id']: task ...}; if any(accepted.get(task['id']) != task for task in declared): raise ValueError('Chapter WBS must preserve every owned manifest declaration exactly')` (store.py:741-743).

Any of these model changes fails the check:
- a reworded description
- a trimmed or added space
- a Unicode change (for example en-dash to hyphen)
- requirement or dependency lists in a different order
- an added field (such as status)
- a dropped field that the manifest model had added (such as dependencies or deliverable)
- a renumbered ID
- narrowed requirements
- an omitted task

All of these were reproduced in process (scratch exp1.py). The ValueError becomes failure category 'code' (runtime.py:382-385). A 'code' failure adds to failure_count and retries the same target, with no fallback and no backoff (routing_store.py:556-571). After max_attempts=3 the job and its whole workflow become BLOCKED (store.py:969-983). The resume path refuses to reset an exhausted budget (store.py:1216-1217).

Chapter drafts get 0 task-kind points (routing.py:406), so they land in tier 1-3: gemini-3.8-flash, then claude-haiku-4-5, then gpt-6-luna low (routing.py:104-105). Before r5, Gemini is not usable, so Haiku carried the whole verbatim-echo burden. It drifted on 13 of about 22 drafts, 3 times each, which blocked 3 of 4 planning workflows. This happened even though the prompt already says "Preserve all supplied WBS declarations exactly" and shows the declarations twice (worker.py:172-182, 285-288). Because the requirement is a model-fidelity requirement placed on controller-owned data, it fails whatever the provider. After r5 the same tier would send drafts to gemini-3.8-flash first.

Secondary latent defect, reproduced in exp2.py:
- Additional (model-added) task IDs are checked for uniqueness only within their own chapter (store.py:708-727).
- Cross-chapter uniqueness is checked only at gather time (store.py:880-885). Gather runs inside the completion of the LAST chapter (store.py:838-839, 845-857).
- So if chapter A appends an ID that equals a sibling's declared ID, A is accepted. The innocent last chapter B then fails every retry with 'Accepted WBS task IDs must retain exactly one owning chapter', and the workflow BLOCKS.

findings.root_cause:
Mostly (b), allocator high-water and fragmentation from large transient read projections, sitting on top of (c), an idle footprint of about 40 MiB that leaves less than 10 MiB of headroom. There is no Python-level leak; one small unbounded per-task growth (a) exists but does not explain the jump. The budget check has no hysteresis in either direction.

(1) Guard. controller_guard.py:15-26 compares one psutil rss sample (the Windows working set, controller_guard.py:43-44) against 50. The sample is cached for at most 1 s (controller_guard.py:37), and the tick runs every 0.1 s (runtime.py:613). runtime.py:454-465 applies the verdict as an overlay that sets capacity 0 AFTER HardwareGuard.evaluate has already run GovernorState.apply (hardware_guard.py:371, 292-325). So one sample over 50 MiB closes admission at once, and the next sample at or under 50 reopens it at once. It bypasses the governor's 10 s / 3-sample recovery and +1-seat ramp (hardware_guard.py:43-46), so admission flaps. private_mb is recorded but never assessed (controller_guard.py:45-46).

(2) Growth drivers.
- /operator (operator_views.py:502-653) loads 200 jobs and 200 events with SELECT * and json.loads (operator_views.py:525-541). Every event carries a full ~7.2 KB host sample, written by routing_store.py:235-266 from store.set_transition_telemetry (store.py:394-397). resource_plot copies the full 'measurements' into every point (operator_views.py:284), and acceptance_dashboard re-reads and re-hashes the specification artifacts on every call (operator_views.py:581, 114-212). The result is about 1.1 MB of JSON (fixture: 1,121,808 bytes; resources 557 KB, acceptance 386 KB). It is encoded with ensure_ascii=False into a 2-byte-per-char str and then into bytes (service.py:87-95). Python peak per call is about 18 MB (tracemalloc), and up to 16 requests may run concurrently (service.py:54). The pymalloc arenas that are released never return: 19 arenas (19.9 MB) after sequential calls and 36-37 arenas (37.7 MB) after concurrent calls, with only 11.8 MB live both times.
- Each per-call read connection uses the default 2 MiB page cache (store.py:303-325). The persistent writer cache adds about 2.4 MiB of SQLite heap at steady state.
- The knowledge reader pool (knowledge.py:276, 476-491) keeps up to 2 immutable readers with cache_size=-8192. The 30 s background refresh runs PRAGMA quick_check over the whole index (knowledge.py:508-511; runtime.py:605-607), so each pooled reader caches the entire index. Measured 2.22 MiB per reader at a 2.0 MB index; the live index is 3,747,840 bytes, so about 4.1 MiB per reader and up to about 8 MiB for two (extrapolated).

(3) Leak (a). Python-level live memory is flat: tracemalloc current is 10.25-10.32 MB across 100 sequential and 24 concurrent operator calls. The only unbounded structure found is Oracle._rates / _last_seen per task id (oracle.py:299-301, 399-406), pruned only on a trip, at about 0.8 KB per job. It does not explain the 40-to-54 MiB jump.

(4) Fixture reproduction of the live symptom. Idle with server is 40-41 MiB. Sequential /operator polling plateaus at 47.7-50.3 MiB. Four concurrent pollers reach 61.8-63.4 MiB, and after 24 concurrent calls the process stays at about 70 MiB working set / 57 MiB private. Live r4 now reads 43.9-44.3 MiB rss and 51.7-52.2 MiB private with no active jobs, and private rose 0.48 MiB in 14 idle minutes.

findings.root_cause: The mechanism is established; the specific cause for job 339ade14 is not. Job 339ade14f7ee44639176a1d8e9c61e14 (CHAPTER_DRAFT, workflow 0213cc0c4da342faa1b9317e4a2552ea, routed to claude:claude-haiku-4-5 after the Gemini candidate was skipped for compatibility, bound to slot6) failed three times. Each attempt lasted about 12 s (12.6, 11.7 and 11.5 s), against 24-58 s for the sibling haiku chapters that succeeded on other slots in the same minute. Every failure was ProviderFailure('code'). In the installed r4 code that category can only come from the inference step, after the controller's own per-attempt checks had passed. Those checks are the Claude --help policy probe, which would raise 'compatibility', and `claude ... auth status --json` in the slot6 profile, which would raise 'auth' (or 'compatibility' for the cache report). So 'code' means one of two things. Either the Claude CLI exited nonzero without any recognised native failure envelope (worker.py:862-863), or it emitted a result record with is_error=true whose cause sits only in its `result` text, which failures.py never inspects, so it falls back to 'code' (failures.py:165-173, 196-209). I checked this against the installed r4 failures.py: Claude result envelopes whose text is 'API Error: 401 ...', 'Invalid API key', 'API Error: 529 ...' or 'API Error: 429 ...' all classify as ('code', None). Because 'code' is not an availability category, it counted against the job's failure budget on the same slot-bound route instead of placing a hold and rerouting. The job hit the three-failure poison pill in 37 s. The real diagnosis exists only in SYSTEM-only per-attempt logs under C:\ProgramData\CoChemPipeline427\private\attempts\<attempt_id>\ (auth.out, auth.err, stdout.log, stderr.log). The public API redacts attempt_id, the native exit code is never recorded for a failed attempt, and the job and slot6 are confounded because a chapter stays bound to its first slot. One hypothesis is ruled out for 22:17-22:18: an explicitly logged-out slot6 session, which would have produced category 'auth'. Five remain open until the logs are copied: (H1) a server-side expired or revoked Claude token while local credentials still report loggedIn; (H2) a rate limit or overload reported only in result text; (H3) a job-specific API rejection or refusal; (H4) a slot6-local CLI crash (profile, config or RAM-disk project cache); (H5) any other nonzero exit with no JSON. The 2026-10-08 status receipts show slot6 Claude logged in at 20:47 and slot6 Codex logged in at 20:39.
